name: Mint
description: A vigorous perennial herb with a refreshing flavor. Popular for teas, cocktails, and culinary uses. Spreads rapidly by underground runners.
tips: Plant in containers to prevent it from taking over the garden. Pinch flowers to maintain leaf production. Divide plants every 2-3 years.
succession: Not necessary; perennial plant spreads and produces continuously.
harvestInstructions: Harvest stems and leaves as needed. Cut stems back to just above a leaf node to encourage bushier growth. Harvest frequently to keep the plant in check.
containerGardening: Highly recommended to prevent aggressive spreading. Use any size pot with good drainage, but be aware it will quickly fill it. Keep well-watered.

soil.type: Moist, well-drained soil rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Tolerates various soil types but prefers consistently moist conditions.

temperature.notes: Cool-season perennial. Dies back in winter but returns in spring in zones 3-9.

environmentalAlerts.message: Increase watering - mint requires consistent moisture to prevent wilting.

storage: Keep fresh stems in a glass of water. Dries well for teas. Can be chopped and frozen in ice cube trays with water or oil.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep soil consistently moist and provide partial shade for young plants.

careTasks.name: First harvest
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting leaves when plants are 4-6 inches tall.

careTasks.name: Pinch flowers
careTasks.description: Remove flower buds to encourage leaf production and prevent seeding.

careTasks.name: Harvest leaves
careTasks.description: Harvest regularly by cutting stems just above leaf pairs to encourage bushier growth.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water frequently to maintain consistently moist soil. Mulch around plants to retain moisture.

name: Rosemary
plantingDepth: 1/4 inch deep, but starting from cuttings is much easier and more reliable.
description: A woody, aromatic perennial herb with needle-like leaves. Essential for Mediterranean cooking and valued for its fragrant, pine-like scent.
tips: Protect from harsh winter winds. Prune after flowering to maintain shape. Excellent in containers for colder climates.
succession: Not necessary; evergreen perennial provides year-round harvest where hardy.
harvestInstructions: Harvest sprigs by cutting them off the plant. Do not cut back into the old, woody growth, as it may not regrow. Harvest regularly once the plant is established.
containerGardening: Excellent for containers, especially in cold climates where it must be brought indoors for winter. Ensure superb drainage to prevent root rot.

soil.type: Well-drained, sandy soil. Poor to moderately fertile.
soil.notes: Excellent drainage is essential. Tolerates drought and poor soils once established.

temperature.notes: Hardy in zones 7-10. In colder zones, grow in containers and bring indoors for winter.

environmentalAlerts.message: In zones 6 and below, move containers indoors or provide winter protection.
Ensure good drainage to prevent root rot in wet conditions.

storage: Can be hung in bundles to air dry. Fresh sprigs last 1-2 weeks in the refrigerator. Also freezes well, either loose or in oil.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Provide bottom heat and ensure excellent drainage for slow-germinating seeds.

careTasks.name: First light harvest
careTasks.description: Begin light harvesting once plant is well-established with woody stems.

careTasks.name: Pruning
careTasks.description: Prune lightly to maintain shape and encourage new growth. Avoid cutting into old wood.

careTasks.name: Regular harvest
careTasks.description: Harvest sprigs by cutting stems just above leaf nodes. Never harvest more than 1/3 of the plant.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water sparingly, allowing soil to dry between waterings. Overwatering can cause root rot.

name: Thyme
plantingDepth: 1/4 inch deep, barely cover as seeds need light to germinate.
description: A low-growing perennial herb with small, aromatic leaves. Essential in French cuisine and herb blends. Forms dense, spreading mats.
tips: Trim back after flowering to maintain compact growth. Divide clumps every 3-4 years to rejuvenate plants.
succession: Not necessary; perennial provides continuous harvest.
harvestInstructions: Cut fresh sprigs as needed throughout the season. For a large harvest for drying, cut the plant back by about half just before it begins to flower for the most intense flavor.
containerGardening: Grows well in pots, especially creeping varieties which will spill over the sides. Needs excellent drainage and a gritty soil mix.

soil.type: Well-drained, light soil. Tolerates poor, rocky soils.
soil.notes: Excellent drainage is crucial. Thrives in lean soils with good drainage.

temperature.notes: Hardy perennial in zones 4-9. Tolerates cold well but may die back in severe winters.

environmentalAlerts.message: Improve drainage to prevent root rot and fungal issues.

storage: Dries exceptionally well and retains flavor. Hang small bundles in a well-ventilated area. Can also be frozen on the stem.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Seeds are tiny and slow to germinate. Keep soil lightly moist but not waterlogged.

careTasks.name: First harvest
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting when plants are well-established and 4-6 inches tall.

careTasks.name: Post-bloom trim
careTasks.description: Trim back by one-third after flowering to encourage fresh growth and prevent woodiness.

careTasks.name: Regular harvest
careTasks.description: Cut sprigs regularly to encourage branching. Harvest in morning after dew dries.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water moderately, allowing soil to dry between waterings. Very drought tolerant once established.

name: Oregano
plantingDepth: 1/4 inch deep, surface sow as seeds need light.
description: A robust perennial herb with pungent, earthy flavor essential in Mediterranean and Italian cooking. Forms spreading clumps with small white or pink flowers.
tips: Pinch flowers to maintain leaf quality. Divide plants every 3 years. Greek oregano has the strongest flavor for cooking.
succession: Not necessary; perennial provides season-long harvest.
harvestInstructions: Cut sprigs as needed. The flavor is most intense just before the plant flowers. For a large harvest for drying, cut the plant back to a few inches from the ground.
containerGardening: Grows well in containers. A 1-2 gallon pot is sufficient. It tends to spread, so a wide pot is a good choice.

soil.notes: Tolerates poor soils. Good drainage prevents root rot in winter.

temperature.notes: Hardy perennial in zones 5-10. May die back in winter but returns in spring.

environmentalAlerts.message: Ensure good drainage to prevent winter kill and root rot.

storage: Dries very well and is the most common way to preserve it. Hang in small bundles to air dry. Can also be frozen in oil or water.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep soil consistently moist until germination. Seedlings are slow to establish.

careTasks.name: First harvest
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting when plants are 4-6 inches tall and well-branched.

careTasks.name: Pinch flowers
careTasks.description: Remove flower buds regularly to maintain tender leaves and prevent self-seeding.

careTasks.name: Major harvest
careTasks.description: Cut stems back by half for drying when plants are in full growth before flowering.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water regularly but allow soil to dry slightly between waterings. Avoid overhead watering.

name: Dill
description: A delicate annual herb with feathery foliage and distinctive tangy flavor. Essential for pickles, fish dishes, and European cuisine. Self-seeds readily.
tips: Direct sow only - does not transplant well. Sow every 2-3 weeks for continuous harvest. Allow some plants to flower for dill seeds.
succession: Sow every 2-3 weeks for a continuous supply of fresh leaves (dill weed).
yield: Multiple cuttings per plant before flowering.
harvestInstructions: Harvest feathery leaves (dill weed) anytime during the growing season by snipping them off. For dill seed, let the plant flower and the seed heads turn brown, then cut the entire stalk and hang to dry.
containerGardening: Can be grown in deep pots (at least 12 inches) to accommodate its long taproot. May require staking if it gets tall.

soil.type: Well-drained, fertile soil with good organic matter.
soil.notes: Prefers loose, well-cultivated soil. Avoid heavy clay or waterlogged conditions.

temperature.notes: Cool-season annual. Bolts quickly in hot weather. Best grown in spring and fall.

environmentalAlerts.message: Provide afternoon shade during hot weather to prevent early bolting.

storage: Fresh leaves are best and can be stored in water in the fridge for a week. They can be frozen, but lose flavor when dried. Dried seeds should be stored in an airtight container.

careTasks.name: Direct sowing
careTasks.description: Sow seeds directly in garden. Seeds need light to germinate - barely cover with soil.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart when 2 inches tall. Use thinnings in cooking.

careTasks.name: First harvest
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting leaves when plants are 6-8 inches tall.

careTasks.name: Regular harvest
careTasks.description: Cut outer leaves regularly to encourage new growth. Harvest before flowering for best flavor.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water regularly to maintain consistent moisture. Avoid overhead watering to prevent disease.

name: Chives
description: A hardy perennial herb with slender, hollow leaves and mild onion flavor. Produces attractive purple flowers that are also edible. Excellent for containers.
tips: Cut leaves down to 2 inches from the ground for harvesting. Divide clumps every 3-4 years to reinvigorate them. Flowers are edible and make a great garnish.
succession: Not necessary; perennial provides continuous harvest.
harvestInstructions: Harvest leaves by cutting them at the base, about 1-2 inches from the ground. Harvest from the outside of the clump first. Edible flowers can be harvested as they open.
containerGardening: Excellent for containers. A 6-8 inch pot is a good size. Can be kept on a sunny windowsill through winter.

soil.type: Well-drained, fertile soil rich in organic matter.
soil.notes: Adaptable to various soil types but prefers moist, well-drained conditions.

temperature.notes: Very hardy perennial in zones 3-9. Goes dormant in winter.

storage: Best used fresh. Store cut leaves in a plastic bag in the refrigerator for up to a week. They freeze well when chopped, but do not retain flavor when dried.

careTasks.name: Care for Seedlings
careTasks.description: Keep soil moist. Seedlings are slow to establish but very hardy once mature.

careTasks.name: Harvest leaves
careTasks.description: Cut outer leaves about 2 inches from the ground. Regular harvesting encourages new growth.

careTasks.name: Divide clumps
careTasks.description: Every 3-4 years, dig up and divide clumps in spring to rejuvenate them.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water regularly, especially during dry spells. Chives prefer consistent moisture.
